Content.Title: Fully Defined Sketches
Content.Description: All sketch entities must be fully constrained to prevent accidental geometry shifts.

Content.Title: Material Specification and Density
Content.Description: Assign correct material from the library to ensure accurate mass property calculations.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Material drives weight, center of gravity, moment of inertia, and FEA yield strength. An incorrect or missing material assignment means all mass property reports, lifting calculations, and simulation results are wrong. Procurement may also order the wrong alloy if the part file does not carry the correct material metadata. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Open the part file, right-click \b Material \b0 in the Feature Tree, and select \b Edit Material \b0. \line \bullet Choose from the company-approved library. Do not create custom materials without engineering approval. \line \bullet Verify the density value matches the certified material data sheet (MDS/CoC). \line \bullet For assemblies, run \b Evaluate -> Mass Properties \b0 and cross-check total weight against hand calculations. \line \line }

Content.Title: Draft Analysis for Tooling
Content.Description: Ensure vertical faces have sufficient draft angles for part removal from molds.

Content.Title: Tree Organization and Naming Convention
Content.Description: Rename critical features and sub-assemblies for clarity and faster troubleshooting.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Default names like 'Boss-Extrude1' or 'Cut-Extrude3' give no information about function. When someone else opens your model six months later, or when a PDM workflow audit is performed, an unreadable feature tree wastes hours of investigation time. Clear names also make suppress/unsuppress operations and configurations far safer to manage. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Slow double-click any feature in the tree to rename it inline. Use underscores (no spaces): \b Main_Body, Mounting_Boss, Thread_Cut_M8 \b0. \line \bullet Rename sub-assemblies that represent functional groups: 'Drive_Unit', 'Frame_Weldment'. \line \bullet Group fasteners into folders: right-click -> \b Add to New Folder \b0. \line \bullet Apply consistent prefixes: CUT_ for cuts, REF_ for reference geometry, SHT_ for sheet metal. \line \line }

Content.Title: Standard Hole Wizard Implementation
Content.Description: Use Hole Wizard for all fastener holes to maintain thread and clearance standards.

Content.Title: Interference and Clearance Detection
Content.Description: Verify that no two components occupy the same physical space.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Physical interferences discovered during prototype build or production assembly result in immediate rework, schedule delays, and cost overruns. CAD software can detect these in seconds. There is no excuse for releasing an assembly with unresolved hard interferences. Clearance issues in dynamic (moving) assemblies can also cause noise, wear, or failure in service. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Run \b Evaluate -> Interference Detection \b0 before every release. Set 'Include multibody part interferences'. \line \bullet Resolve all \b Hard Interferences \b0 (red). These are real clashes that will prevent assembly. \line \bullet Review \b Coincident \b0 results - these may be intentional press-fits. Document press-fits in the notes. \line \bullet For moving parts, use \b Evaluate -> Clearance Verification \b0 and check at end-of-travel positions. \line \line }

Content.Title: Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T)
Content.Description: Apply GD&T to define functional requirements on technical drawings.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Coordinate tolerances (+/- dimensions) are ambiguous at the inspection stage and often over-constrain the part, increasing cost unnecessarily. GD&T communicates the actual functional requirement: how much can a surface tilt, shift, or deviate while the part still works? Without GD&T, the manufacturing shop interprets drawing intent subjectively, and QC rejects good parts or accepts bad ones. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Establish a Datum Reference Frame (DRF) using three mutually perpendicular datums: A (primary), B (secondary), C (tertiary). \line \bullet Apply Position tolerance to all mating holes. Apply Flatness or Parallelism to sealing and mating faces. \line \bullet Follow \b ASME Y14.5-2018 \b0 or \b ISO 1101 \b0 - confirm which standard applies to the customer or manufacturing country. \line \bullet Use the GD&T annotation tools in the drawing environment and link them to model datums for 3D MBD workflows. \line \line }

Content.Title: Base Component Fixation
Content.Description: The primary component of an assembly must be fixed to the origin.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line If the base component is not fixed, the entire assembly can translate or rotate in space. This causes all mates to become redundant, mate errors during rebuild, and incorrect mass property origins. It also means mating new components to the floating base will produce unpredictable results and confusing error messages. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Insert the base component first. Right-click it in the Feature Tree -> \b Fix \b0. The (f) prefix will appear. \line \bullet Alternatively, use a \b Coincident mate \b0 between the part origin and the assembly origin for a more flexible approach (allows configuration overrides). \line \bullet Confirm the base component does not show any degrees of freedom in \b Evaluate -> Assembly Statistics \b0. \line \bullet Never fix a non-base component. Over-fixing creates a rigid assembly that cannot be re-mated if geometry changes. \line \line }

Content.Title: BOM Metadata Accuracy - DEMO
Content.Description: Fill all Custom Properties (Description, Part Number, Vendor) in the model file.

Content.Title: Simplified Feature Configurations
Content.Description: Create simplified versions of complex parts for large assemblies.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line In assemblies with 500+ components, detailed geometry (fillets, threads, logos, internal pockets) multiplies the graphics triangle count by an order of magnitude. This slows rotation, mate solving, and rebuild times to unusable levels. Engineers spend more time waiting than designing. A simplified configuration suppresses non-functional features and restores interactive performance without losing any engineering data. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet In the part, create a new configuration called 'Simplified' alongside 'Default'. \line \bullet In 'Simplified', suppress all aesthetic fillets, chamfers, threads, cosmetic features, and logos. Keep only the outer envelope geometry. \line \bullet In the assembly, right-click the component -> \b Component Properties \b0 -> select 'Simplified' configuration. \line \bullet Alternatively, use \b SpeedPak \b0: right-click sub-assembly -> Create SpeedPak. This generates a mesh-only proxy with exact geometry for display. \line \line }

Content.Title: Projection Angle Clarity
Content.Description: Clearly define 1st Angle vs 3rd Angle projection on drawings.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line First Angle (ISO/European) and Third Angle (ANSI/US) projection place views on opposite sides of the front view. If the symbol is missing or wrong and the drawing is sent to a manufacturer in a different region, they may machine a mirrored part. This is an irreversible error on machined or formed components and results in 100% scrap. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Set the projection angle in \b Sheet Properties \b0 (right-click the sheet background). \line \bullet Ensure the projection symbol is visible in the Title Block area. Do not hide or crop it. \line \bullet For international suppliers, add a text note: 'UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED, THIRD ANGLE PROJECTION'. \line \bullet If your template does not include a projection symbol, update it before releasing any drawings outside the company. \line \line }

Content.Title: Fillet and Chamfer Hierarchy
Content.Description: Place non-functional aesthetic features at the very end of the tree.

Content.Title: Standard Parts Library Usage
Content.Description: Always use approved library (Toolbox) for fasteners and hardware.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Manually modeled fasteners create duplicate part files with inconsistent properties, wrong dimensions, and no link to the ERP item master. Each engineer reinvents the same M8 bolt differently. Toolbox parts share a single file with configurations for every size, automatically carry correct metadata, and maintain BOM accuracy. Using custom screw models inflates assembly file count and breaks procurement workflows. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Access fasteners via \b Design Library -> Toolbox \b0 only. Never model screws, nuts, or washers manually. \line \bullet Configure Toolbox with company-approved part numbers mapped to each fastener standard (e.g., DIN 912 M8x20 -> PN: FST-0082-020). \line \bullet If a required fastener is not in Toolbox, submit a request to the CAD administrator to add it - do not create a workaround. \line \bullet Toolbox parts must reference the PDM vault path, not a local drive. Confirm the Toolbox path in \b Tools -> Options -> System Options -> Hole Wizard/Toolbox \b0. \line \line }

Content.Title: Revision History Management
Content.Description: Document every drawing change in the revision table.

Content.Title: Symmetry and Mirror Utilization
Content.Description: Use mirrors to maintain symmetry and reduce design time.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Modeling symmetrical geometry twice doubles both modeling time and the risk of inconsistency. If the original side is later modified, the manually copied side must be updated separately. Using Mirror ensures that both sides are always identical by definition, and changes to the original automatically propagate. This is especially critical for structural parts where asymmetry introduces unexpected stress concentrations. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet In parts, use \b Insert -> Pattern/Mirror -> Mirror Features \b0, selecting a plane of symmetry and the features to mirror. \line \bullet For bodies, use \b Mirror Bodies \b0 and choose 'Merge solids' if the result should be a single body. \line \bullet In assemblies, use \b Insert -> Mirror Components \b0. Choose 'Create opposite hand version' only when a physically mirrored part is needed (left/right hand). Otherwise use 'Reuse components' to place the same part on both sides. \line \bullet Confirm the mirror plane is associated with the correct reference geometry, not a temporary sketch plane. \line \line }

Content.Title: Dimension Redundancy
Content.Description: Do not define the same feature twice in a drawing view.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Duplicate dimensions on a drawing create an inspection ambiguity: if the two instances of the same dimension are ever different (due to a missed update after a model change), the drawing becomes internally contradictory. The inspector does not know which value governs. This can lead to scrapped parts or legal disputes. Redundant dimensions also clutter the drawing and slow down reading time. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Each dimension should appear in exactly one view - the one where it is most clearly visible and interpretable. \line \bullet If a dimension must appear in a second view for clarity, mark it as a Reference dimension with the (REF) suffix. Reference dimensions are non-governing and shown in parentheses. \line \bullet Use \b Ordinate Dimensioning \b0 for hole patterns to eliminate chain accumulation and reduce the number of annotations. \line \bullet After any model change, use \b Tools -> Model Items \b0 to import updated dimensions and delete any that have become duplicates. \line \line }

Content.Title: Assembly Mate Simplification
Content.Description: Use simplest mates (Profile Center, Width) to reduce solve time.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Every mate adds an equation the solver must process during rebuild. Complex advanced mates (Path Mate, Gear Mate, Cam Mate) are computationally expensive and can create circular references that cause the assembly to fail to rebuild or produce incorrect positions. Over-constrained assemblies with redundant mates are fragile and produce wrong interference results. The goal is the minimum number of mates that fully define the component position. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Prefer \b Coincident, Concentric, and Parallel \b0 over complex advanced mates wherever possible. \line \bullet Use \b Profile Center \b0 mate to center a component between two parallel faces in a single mate instead of two symmetric mates. \line \bullet Never add a mate that turns a component red (over-defined). Investigate and remove the conflicting mate immediately. \line \bullet Run \b Evaluate -> Assembly Statistics \b0 after mating. Review the 'Redundant constraints' count and aim for zero. \line \line }

Content.Title: Virtual Sharps for Radiused Edges
Content.Description: Define theoretical intersection points for accurate dimensioning.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line When a corner is filleted or chamfered, the original sharp corner no longer exists in the model. Dimensioning to a tangent point on a fillet arc is meaningless to manufacturing because the arc location shifts with tolerance. The virtual sharp reconstructs the theoretical sharp corner, giving the machinist and inspector a stable, unambiguous reference point that does not move with radius variation. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet In the drawing view, click the two edges that would have met at the sharp corner. \line \bullet Go to \b Tools -> Sketch Entities -> Point \b0 while in sketch mode to add a virtual sharp marker, or right-click the intersection -> \b Insert Virtual Sharp \b0. \line \bullet A small 'X' marker appears at the theoretical intersection. Snap dimensions to this marker, not to the fillet arc. \line \bullet This is mandatory for sheet metal parts where bend inspection is performed from the virtual sharp of the bend tangent lines. \line \line }

Content.Title: Tolerance Stack-up Prevention
Content.Description: Use baseline dimensioning to prevent cumulative manufacturing errors.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line In chain dimensioning, each feature is located relative to the previous one. The tolerance of each link adds to the total. In a chain of 5 features each with +/-0.1mm tolerance, the last feature has a worst-case position error of +/-0.5mm. Baseline dimensioning references every feature back to a single datum, so tolerances do not accumulate. This is not optional when functional requirements are tight. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Identify the functional datum: the surface or hole from which all other features must be accurately located. \line \bullet Dimension all features directly from this datum. Use \b Ordinate Dimensions \b0 in the drawing to display this compactly without clutter. \line \bullet Conduct a formal tolerance stack-up analysis (worst-case or RSS method) for critical fits, especially for mating bores and shafts. \line \bullet If chain dimensioning appears on any existing drawing, add a note specifying which dimension is non-governing, or redimension using baseline method. \line \line }

Content.Title: Center of Gravity (COG) Awareness
Content.Description: Verify COG for stability and safe lifting points.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line An assembly lifted from incorrect points will tilt, placing unintended loads on the structure and creating a safety hazard for personnel. Machines with a high or offset COG can tip over during transport if not properly restrained. Regulatory frameworks (machinery directive, CE marking) require lifting point analysis for equipment above certain weight thresholds. An incorrect COG in CAD also means the structural analysis results are wrong. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Run \b Evaluate -> Mass Properties \b0 on the fully mated assembly. Note the COG coordinates. \line \bullet Verify that all components have correct materials assigned before reading the COG - a part with no material has zero density and skews the result. \line \bullet For parts over 20 kg and assemblies over 50 kg, add the COG symbol and coordinates to the drawing using a general note or dedicated view. \line \bullet Confirm lifting eyes or rigging points are positioned above and symmetric to the COG. Engage the structural engineer if the COG is offset. \line \line }

Content.Title: Surface Finish Callouts
Content.Description: Define required roughness (Ra) for functional surfaces.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Without a surface finish callout, the manufacturing shop applies its default machining finish, which may be completely wrong for the function. A sealing surface that needs Ra 0.8 machined to Ra 6.3 will leak. A bearing journal machined too smooth (Ra 0.1) will not retain lubrication. Surface finish affects sealing, friction, fatigue life, corrosion resistance, and coating adhesion. Every functional surface needs an explicit callout. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Use ISO 1302 surface finish symbols in the drawing. \line \bullet Apply the general surface finish in the Title Block (e.g., Ra 3.2 unless otherwise noted). \line \bullet Override with specific callouts on functional surfaces: Ra 0.8 for O-ring grooves and seal faces, Ra 1.6 for hydraulic cylinder bores, Ra 3.2 for general machining, Ra 6.3 for non-contact surfaces. \line \bullet Specify the machining lay direction (= parallel, X crossed, C circular) where tribology or sealing requires it. \line \line }

Content.Title: Hardware Pattern Utilization
Content.Description: Use Pattern features for fasteners to ensure sync.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Manually placed fasteners in a bolt circle must be individually updated if the hole pattern changes. A bolt circle with 8 manually placed bolts requires 8 separate edits when the pitch diameter changes. A pattern-driven component pattern updates all instances automatically by following the Hole Wizard pattern in the part. This eliminates count mismatches between holes and bolts - a dangerous and embarrassing error. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet In the part, create all holes using a single \b Circular or Linear Pattern \b0 of a Hole Wizard feature. \line \bullet In the assembly, insert one bolt, nut, and washer set and fully mate it to the first hole. \line \bullet Use \b Insert -> Component Pattern -> Pattern Driven \b0 and select the hole pattern as the driver. All remaining holes are populated with correctly mated instances automatically. \line \bullet When the hole count changes in the part, the component pattern updates at next rebuild - no manual assembly work required. \line \line }

Content.Title: Internal Radii (Sharp Corner Avoidance)
Content.Description: Provide internal radii to reduce stress concentration.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Sharp internal corners (zero radius) are stress risers. Under cyclic loading, cracks initiate at stress concentrations and propagate to fracture. The stress concentration factor (Kt) at a perfectly sharp corner is theoretically infinite. Even a small radius of 0.5mm can reduce the stress concentration by 30-50% depending on geometry. This directly extends fatigue life. Sharp corners also make CNC machining impossible without a corner relief. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Define the minimum internal radius early in the sketch, not as a fillet feature, for pockets that must match a tool radius. \line \bullet Match the radius to the nearest standard end-mill size: 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10mm. Odd radii require special tooling at extra cost. \line \bullet For high-cycle fatigue parts (>10^6 cycles), perform FEA to confirm the selected radius brings peak stress below the material endurance limit. \line \bullet Call out radii explicitly on the drawing. Do not rely on 'break all sharp edges' general notes for structural internal corners. \line \line }

Content.Title: Exploded View and Ballooning
Content.Description: Create exploded views for assembly manuals.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Assembly technicians and field service engineers rely on exploded views to understand the assembly sequence without reading text instructions. A correctly ballooned exploded view with a matching BOM reduces assembly errors, speeds up training of new staff, and is a contractual deliverable for many OEM and end-customer relationships. Without it, customer support receives unnecessary calls and warranty claims. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Create the exploded view in the assembly using \b Insert -> Exploded View \b0. Explode along logical assembly axes. \line \bullet In the drawing, insert the exploded view configuration via \b Insert -> Model View \b0, then select the exploded state. \line \bullet Add balloons via \b Insert -> Annotations -> Balloon \b0. Use 'Magnetic Line' to align balloons cleanly along the drawing edge. \line \bullet Number balloons in assembly sequence order (1 = first part installed). Link the balloon numbers to a BOM table so part numbers and descriptions are captured automatically. \line \line }

Content.Title: File Reference Integrity (Broken Links)
Content.Description: Ensure all component references are resolved and no Suppress state is accidental.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line A broken reference (shown as a '?' in the Feature Tree) means the assembly cannot find a referenced file. The affected component is displayed as a phantom and contributes nothing to mass properties, interference detection, or the BOM. If this reaches the drawing stage, views appear empty or show outdated geometry. In PDM, releasing a file with broken references creates an incomplete revision that can never be fully reconstructed. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Before releasing, open the assembly and check the Feature Tree for any '?' symbols next to components. \line \bullet Use \b File -> Find References \b0 to see every file the assembly depends on and confirm all paths are valid vault locations. \line \bullet If a reference is broken, use \b Replace Component \b0 or \b File -> Open -> References \b0 to re-point to the correct file. \line \bullet Confirm no components are accidentally suppressed (grey text in tree). A suppressed structural component is invisible to interference detection and missing from the BOM. \line \line }

Content.Title: Sheet Metal Bend Parameters
Content.Description: Define K-Factor and Bend Radius accurately.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line The K-Factor determines where the neutral axis sits within the material thickness during bending, which in turn determines the correct blank (flat pattern) length. An incorrect K-Factor produces a flat pattern that is either too short or too long, causing the bent part to be out of tolerance. This error is only discovered after the blank has been laser-cut and sent to the press brake - resulting in 100% scrap of the cut blanks. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Obtain the K-Factor from the press brake operator or from the machine tooling data sheet for each material and thickness combination. Typical range: 0.30 (tight bend, thin material) to 0.50 (large radius, thick material). \line \bullet Set the K-Factor in \b Sheet Metal feature -> Bend Allowance -> K-Factor \b0. Do not use the default 0.5 without verification. \line \bullet The minimum inside bend radius must be at least equal to the material thickness for steel. Using a tighter radius causes cracking on the outside of the bend. \line \bullet Include the flat pattern as a separate drawing view or as a DXF export. Label it 'FLAT PATTERN - DO NOT SCALE' with the blank dimensions clearly stated. \line \line }

Content.Title: Weldment Cut List Management
Content.Description: Use structural members and cut lists for frames.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line Weldment frames modeled as individual part files in an assembly require manual length tracking, separate drawings for each tube, and a handmade cut list. The Weldments environment automates this: it generates a Cut List with quantities, lengths, and profiles for every structural member, and feeds this directly into a drawing Cut List Table. This eliminates counting errors and saves hours of documentation work on every frame design. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Model the frame centreline skeleton as a 3D sketch, then apply \b Insert -> Weldments -> Structural Member \b0 to sweep profiles along the paths. \line \bullet After all members are placed, right-click the Cut List folder in the Feature Tree and select \b Update \b0. Review for correct grouping. \line \bullet Add custom properties (Description, Material, Finish) to the Cut List folder for each unique profile type. These propagate to the drawing table. \line \bullet In the drawing, insert a \b Cut List Table \b0 instead of a standard BOM. This automatically lists all members by profile, length, and quantity. \line \line }

Content.Title: Rigid vs Flexible Sub-Assemblies
Content.Description: Optimize memory by keeping sub-assemblies rigid.
Content.DetailRTF: {\rtf1\ansi\deff0 {\fonttbl{\f0 Segoe UI;}} \b WHY? \b0 \line When a sub-assembly is set to Flexible, the parent assembly must solve all internal mates of that sub-assembly on every rebuild. For a complex sub-assembly with many mates, this multiplies the solver load for every instance placed in the parent. In a large assembly with 10 instances of a flexible sub-assembly, the solver is running the sub-assembly mate equations 10 times per rebuild instead of once. This is the most common cause of assembly slowness that is not due to graphics. \line \line \b HOW? \b0 \line \bullet Keep all sub-assemblies in \b Rigid \b0 mode (default) during normal design work. \line \bullet Switch to \b Flexible \b0 only when kinematic motion simulation is needed (e.g., showing a pneumatic cylinder extending). \line \bullet After completing the motion check or animation, immediately return the sub-assembly to Rigid. Add a reminder note in the assembly custom properties if Flexible mode is temporarily required. \line \bullet Right-click the sub-assembly in the tree -> \b Component Properties \b0 -> set Solve as: Rigid or Flexible. \line \line }

Content.Title: Thread Representation Efficiency
Content.Description: Use cosmetic threads instead of modeled 3D threads.
